subject: ela
description: Students demonstrate command of standard English grammar and usage when writing and speaking. They identify and correctly use pronoun case (subjective, objective, possessive); recognize and use intensive pronouns (myself, ourselves); correct inappropriate shifts in pronoun number and person; recognize and correct vague pronouns with ambiguous or missing antecedents; and recognize variations from standard English in their own and others' writing, choosing the correct form to improve expression. Every item embeds the full sentence or short passage it depends on, so the student needs nothing external.
subSkills: Use pronouns in the correct case: subjective (I, he, she, we, they), objective (me, him, her, us, them), and possessive (my, his, her, our, their)
Identify and use intensive pronouns correctly (myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves)
Recognize and correct inappropriate shifts in pronoun number (singular to plural) and person (first to second to third)
Recognize and correct vague pronouns that have ambiguous antecedents or no clear antecedent
Recognize variations from standard English in one's own and others' writing and speaking, and identify strategies to improve expression in conventional language

problemArchetypes.name: Pronoun case selection
problemArchetypes.example: Read the sentence: 'My brother and (I / me) walked to the store after dinner.' Which pronoun is correct? Answer: I, because it is part of the subject performing the action.

problemArchetypes.name: Identify the intensive pronoun and its function
problemArchetypes.example: Read the sentence: 'The principal herself handed out the awards at the assembly.' What does the word 'herself' do in this sentence? Answer: It is an intensive pronoun that emphasizes the noun 'principal.'

problemArchetypes.name: Correct an inappropriate pronoun shift
problemArchetypes.example: Read the sentence: 'When a student finishes the test, they should turn it in quietly.' Rewrite or choose the version that fixes the shift in number. Answer: 'When students finish the test, they should turn it in quietly.'

problemArchetypes.name: Identify and fix a vague pronoun
problemArchetypes.example: Read the sentence: 'Maria told Jen that she had won the contest.' Why is this sentence unclear, and how can it be fixed? Answer: 'she' is vague because it could mean Maria or Jen; rewrite as 'Maria told Jen that Jen had won the contest.'

problemArchetypes.name: Choose the standard-English form within a short passage
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage: 'Me and Devon studied for hours. Us two felt ready for the quiz.' Which revision follows standard English? Answer: 'Devon and I studied for hours. We two felt ready for the quiz.'

Easy.description: A single short sentence (one clause, roughly 8 to 14 words) embedded in the item. The task is to identify or select the correct pronoun or pronoun type. Only one grammar concept is tested, the error or choice is obvious, and the correct answer is in the subjective/objective case or a clearly emphasizing intensive pronoun.
constraints: Stimulus is one simple sentence included in the prompt
Tests exactly one concept (case OR intensive OR an obvious vague reference)
Identify-level task: pick the correct word or name the pronoun type
No multi-step reasoning; the antecedent is named and nearby

Medium.description: A compound or complex sentence, or two related sentences (roughly 15 to 30 words total), embedded in the item. The task requires analysis: correcting a pronoun shift in number or person, or resolving a vague pronoun where two possible antecedents appear. The student must explain or select the corrected version, not just spot a single word.
constraints: Stimulus is a compound/complex sentence or a two-sentence pair in the prompt
Tests pronoun shifts (number or person) or ambiguous antecedents with two candidates
Analyze-level task: choose or produce the corrected version

Hard.description: A short multi-sentence passage (roughly 3 to 5 sentences, 40 to 70 words) embedded in the item that contains more than one usage problem or a subtle one. The task requires evaluation: judging which revision best follows standard English, explaining why a usage choice improves expression, or correcting interacting errors (for example a case error plus a shift). Requires inference about the intended meaning to choose the correct antecedent.
constraints: Stimulus is a 3 to 5 sentence passage included in the prompt
Contains multiple or interacting usage issues, or a subtle standard-English variation
Evaluate-level task: select the best full revision and justify the convention
Requires inference to determine intended meaning and correct antecedent

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student uses the objective case in a compound subject (the 'me and him' error)
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects 'Me and Devon studied' or 'Him and I went' instead of the subjective 'Devon and I studied'

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student uses the subjective case in a compound object (overcorrection)
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects 'between you and I' or 'gave it to she and I' instead of the objective 'between you and me'

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses an intensive pronoun with a reflexive pronoun, or thinks 'myself' can replace 'I' or 'me' as a subject or object
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Treats 'Myself and Jordan finished early' as correct, or labels the emphasizing 'herself' as a reflexive object

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student accepts the singular 'they' with a clearly singular antecedent as a shift error to leave uncorrected, failing to make number agree
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Keeps 'When a student finishes, they turn it in' unchanged instead of matching number (students/they or a student/he or she)

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student does not notice an inappropriate shift in person and lets the sentence drift from third to second person
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Accepts 'If a runner trains hard, you will improve' instead of 'If a runner trains hard, he or she will improve'

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats a vague pronoun as acceptable because a possible antecedent exists somewhere, ignoring the ambiguity between two candidates
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Accepts 'Maria told Jen that she had won' as clear instead of recognizing 'she' could refer to either girl
